summary: Two start-time sources are now compared against each other on Windows by design, and any divergence breaks identity. terminal-agent-control.ts:40-74. On Windows the browse server runs under Node (cli.ts:177-179 hard-requires server-node.mjs; bun-polyfill.cjs supplies Bun.spawn), so process.versions.bun is unset there and every server-side readAgentStartTime/agentProcessInfo falls back to the PowerShell CIM CreationDate. The terminal agent and the compiled CLI run under real Bun and use the new GetProcessTimes reader. Before this commit both sides used the same PowerShell query, so they agreed by construction. Now cross-source comparisons are the normal path: - server.ts:1604 spawnTerminalAgent (Node, PowerShell) passes BROWSE_OWNER_START_TIME to the agent, whose watchdog at terminal-agent.ts:1187 compares it every 15 s with readAgentStartTime(owner) via FFI. A mismatch calls cleanup(), the server's respawn loop (server.ts:1588) starts another agent, and that one also dies at its first watchdog tick: a respawn churn that lasts until the server restarts. - Records written by the CLI (FFI) are judged by the server (PowerShell) in isAgentRecordGone/agentStatus (line 371: startTime mismatch => 'gone'). A false 'gone' makes stopAgentByRecord return true, clearAgentRecord runs and a second agent is spawned while the first is still alive, which violates the "unknown is never gone" invariant the new tests assert. - Records written by the previous release (PowerShell) are read by the upgraded CLI (FFI) on the first run after an upgrade. The only proof of equality is the Windows-only test that compares the two for processes started "now" on a CI image. A known candidate for divergence is the DST fall-back hour: the CIM path turns the DMTF time into a local DateTime and ConvertTo-Json converts it back to UTC. If the ambiguous-DST flag is lost in that round trip, processes started in the first 01:00-02:00 hour come out one hour off, while FILETIME stays exact. The next US fall-back is 2026-11-01, three days out. Verify by running both readers on a Windows host with its clock in that hour. Fix options: make the PowerShell fallback emit raw FILETIME (for example via Get-Process StartTime.ToFileTimeUtc(), or Win32_Process CreationDate parsed with its explicit offset) formatted identically, or normalise both sources to an integer epoch-ms before comparing instead of comparing the "/Date(n)/" strings.

summary: Kill-time ownership on Windows still depends on a 2 s PowerShell spawn, so the flake this commit targets survives on the stop and kill paths. terminal-agent-control.ts:63-68, 381-383, 407-428. agentProcessInfo still runs windowsProcessQuery on every agentStatus call to get the command line. When PowerShell times out under load (the GSTA-139 failure mode), commandLine is '', and agentStatus returns 'unknown' even though the FFI start time matches. As a result, stopAgentByRecord returns false, spawnTerminalAgent refuses the respawn ("identity cannot be confirmed"), and server.ts:1679 shutdown leaves the agent running until its own watchdog notices, up to 15 s later. waitForExit also polls agentStatus every 25 ms, and each poll can block for up to 2 s inside spawnSync. This fails safe (no wrong kill), but the fix is partial: only the start-time half moved in-process. A full fix would read the command line in-process too (NtQueryInformationProcess with ProcessCommandLineInformation) or cache it per (pid, startTime), since the command line cannot change for a fixed process identity.

summary: agentProcessInfo now pays for a PowerShell query whose start time it then throws away, and the two readings are no longer taken in one call. terminal-agent-control.ts:63-68. When FFI succeeds, query.startTime is discarded but the PowerShell process still launches, which is the slow, flaky part. The command line (taken at t1) and the start time (taken at t2) can also come from different processes if the PID is reused in between. I checked whether that can produce a false 'owned' and it cannot: that would need the record's exact start time at t2, which only the original agent has. So this costs latency rather than safety. If finding 2 is fixed by caching the command line per (pid, FFI startTime), check the start time first and skip PowerShell when it already mismatches (that result is 'gone', so no command line is needed).

label: FIXABLE
summary: win32CreationTimeSource.read swallows every FFI failure silently and retries dlopen on every call. terminal-agent-control.ts:41-60. On a Bun build where bun:ffi is unavailable (for example Windows ARM64 without TinyCC support), every call throws inside dlopen, the error is swallowed, and the code quietly falls back to PowerShell. That brings back the exact flake this change removes, with no signal that the fast path is off. Cache the failure (for example win32Kernel = null) and log it once, so a degraded host can be diagnosed.

Start-time identity now mixes two sources on Windows: the Bun agent records and compares FFI GetProcessTimes (exact UTC), while the Node server bundle (no bun:ffi) still uses PowerShell CreationDate, which goes DMTF -> local DateTime -> ConvertTo-Json UTC. For a process created during the fall-back DST overlap hour, .NET resolves the ambiguous local time as standard time, so the two strings differ by one hour. The agent would then treat its live owner as gone (terminal-agent.ts:1187 owner tie), and the Node server's isOurAgent/stopAgentByRecord would refuse to stop an agent whose record holds the FFI value. The Windows equality test only samples current processes, so it cannot catch this.
fix: Make the PowerShell fallback emit the same UTC instant as FFI, for example (Get-Process -Id N).StartTime.ToFileTimeUtc() or the CIM DMTF string parsed with its own offset, and format both through one helper.

summary: "Start time readable" is now treated as "process alive" for exited processes whose kernel object is still referenced. browse/src/terminal-agent-control.ts:40-60 (win32CreationTimeSource.read), consumed at terminal-agent.ts:1187 (owner watchdog) and terminal-agent-control.ts:293 (spawn identity). OpenProcess + GetProcessTimes succeed on a process that has already exited as long as any handle to it remains open (the PID stays reserved, the object lingers). Before this diff the only Windows source was a Win32_Process CIM enumeration, which reports running processes, so an exited owner produced '' and the watchdog fired. Two consumers rely on the start-time read alone, with no separate liveness check: a) Owner watchdog (terminal-agent.ts:1187): `readAgentStartTime(BROWSE_OWNER_PID) !== BROWSE_OWNER_START_TIME` is the only owner-death test. If the browse server dies while something else still holds its handle (the launching CLI process that Bun.spawn'd it and is still running, a debugger, EDR/AV, a job object owner), the FFI read keeps returning the original creation time, the comparison stays equal, and the detached agent never cleans up: an orphaned terminal agent that keeps its port and internal token alive after its owner is gone. b) Spawn path under a Bun spawner (cli.ts:1982/2048 -> spawnTerminalAgent): the spawner holds the child's handle via the Bun.spawn proc object, so a child that crashes immediately still yields a non-empty startTime at line 293. The record is published and the pid is returned as a successful spawn of a dead agent, instead of hitting the "process identity is unavailable" branch. Later status checks fall back to isProcessAlive and report 'gone', so this one degrades to a stale record and a false success rather than corruption. Fix: in read(), also call GetExitCodeProcess on the same handle and return undefined unless the code is STILL_ACTIVE (259), so the FFI source has the same "running processes only" semantics as the CIM query it replaces. Add a win32 test that keeps a handle to an exited child and asserts readAgentStartTime() returns ''.

summary: Cross-source string equality is now load-bearing on the production Windows path, and only same-instant equality is verified. terminal-agent-control.ts:63-74 vs terminal-agent.ts:42/1127/1187 and server.ts:1604. On Windows the daemon runs as server-node.mjs under Node (cli.ts:177 hard-requires it), where process.versions.bun is unset, so the daemon always takes the PowerShell path: ownerStartTime, BROWSE_OWNER_START_TIME and its agentStatus() reads are CIM-derived strings. The terminal agent runs under Bun, so its own record (terminal-agent.ts:1127) and every owner-watchdog read (1187) are FFI-derived strings. Before this diff both sides used the same PowerShell source, so string identity was guaranteed. Now any divergence between "FILETIME/10000 - epoch" and "CIM CreationDate -> local DateTime -> ConvertTo-Json /Date()/" has hard effects: the agent's watchdog sees a mismatch on its first tick and runs cleanup() (the terminal agent kills itself right after every spawn), and the daemon's agentStatus() returns 'gone' (line 371) for a live agent, so stopAgentByRecord() returns true without signalling and spawnTerminalAgent clears the record and starts a second agent next to the live one. The win32-only test covers the current process and a just-spawned child, which proves the ordinary case (ms floor, UTC). It does not cover the local-time round trip in edge cases: a process created inside a DST fall-back ambiguous hour, or before a DST or timezone change and queried after it, where the CIM -> local DateTime -> UTC conversion can be off by the offset delta. The US fall-back is on Nov 1, 2026. Needs someone with a Windows box to confirm whether PowerShell 5.1's conversion preserves the instant across those transitions. If it does not, the robust fix is to normalize both sources to the same numeric value instead of comparing preformatted strings: parse /Date(n)/ on both sides, or have the PowerShell path emit CreationDate.ToFileTimeUtc() ticks.

summary: An FFI-to-PowerShell fallback on the same process flips the identity source mid-lifetime. terminal-agent-control.ts:66-67, 73. A Bun reader that gets an FFI value on one call and falls back to PowerShell on the next (transient OpenProcess failure, dlopen failure on a runtime without bun:ffi support, such as a Windows build where FFI is unavailable) compares strings from two sources. If finding 2's equivalence holds, this is harmless. If not, the same failure modes apply: watchdog self-termination and 'gone' for a live agent. The PowerShell fallback's 2 s timeout returning '' remains the pre-existing failure the diff set out to reduce. It is not new, but it is still how the owner watchdog kills a healthy agent when both sources fail (it treats '' as "owner died"). Worth a counter or log when the fallback is taken, so a drift shows up in diagnostics rather than as unexplained agent restarts.

label: FIXABLE
summary: agentProcessInfo() still spawns PowerShell on every agentStatus() call, including the 25 ms waitForExit polling loop in stopAgentByRecord (terminal-agent-control.ts:412-420), because the command line is still sourced there. With FFI available, a PowerShell timeout no longer empties the start time, but it empties commandLine, so the status becomes 'unknown' and stopAgentByRecord returns false ("refusing a second agent"). This is the safe direction (no signal is sent), but the flaky "terminal unavailable" outcome remains on slow or loaded Windows hosts. The ordering also issues PowerShell before the cheap FFI read, so a dead pid (FFI fails, isAgentRecordLive false) still pays a full PowerShell launch. Reading FFI first and skipping PowerShell when it returns undefined, or reading the command line in-process (NtQueryInformationProcess / ProcessCommandLineInformation), would remove the residual flake.
